item.title: Exoplanets Offer Clues to What Lies Beyond Our Solar System
item.description: Thousands of planets have been discovered beyond our solar system, offering clues to where life might thrive and whether Earth is truly unique.
item.dc:creator: Natalie Wolchover

item.title: Do You Have Questions About A.I.? We Want to Answer Them.
item.description: The New York Times is soliciting readers’ questions about the dangers — and benefits — posed by artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz

item.title: A.I. Queries From Abroad Raise Fears of a Biological Weapons Race
item.description: Today’s chatbots aren’t likely to help lone actors invent a deadly pathogen, experts say. But newer models, trained in biology, may need stronger safeguards.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer
item.media:description: The threat of biological weapons has hung over the world for decades now.

item.title: Most People Don’t Think About Culverts. Their Failure Can Be Deadly.
item.description: Scientists simulated what happens when the pipes and tunnels that divert rainwater fail. In one scenario, 30 percent of local residents couldn’t reach an E.R.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Nazaryan
item.media:credit: Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe, via Getty Images
item.media:description: A volunteer with Berkshire Environmental Action Team during a survey of culvert conditions in Hancock, Mass., in 2024.

item.title: A Mastodon Tooth Is Discovered in a California Creek
item.description: A researcher surveying a San Mateo County creek stumbled upon a preserved Pacific mastodon molar estimated to be at least 10,000 years old.
item.dc:creator: Alena Cerro

item.title: As Millions of Birds Migrate, Residents Are Asked to Turn Off the Lights
item.description: Birds are drawn to lights, and more than a billion die each year after crashing into buildings, experts said.
item.dc:creator: Ishani Desai
item.media:credit: Maddie McGarvey for The New York Times
item.media:description: Birds fill the sky over Ohio in 2025. Tens of millions of migratory birds are expected to take flight Saturday across the Midwest.

item.title: Mercury Is Shrinking, and Faster Than We Thought
item.description: New estimates using the planet’s surface wrinkles show that our smallest planet is growing even smaller, at a faster clip than expected.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.media:credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington
item.media:description: Researchers say the planet might have shrunk by as much as 14.5 miles — nearly a percent off of its current size — since its formation 4.5 billion years ago

item.title: How Did a Heart Drug With So Much Promise Fall So Flat?
item.description: Cardiologists are struggling to figure out why a drug that should have prevented heart attacks didn’t work at all.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:description: An illustration of a lipoprotein A particle. Scientists are asking themselves: If Lp(a) is a marker, what is it marking? Is there another cause of heart disease that no one has thought of?

item.title: A.I. Could Possibly End Humanity. How Are Humans Supposed to Process That?
item.description: The technology is far from the only existential risk our species faces. But weighing such cosmic fears can become a mind-bending exercise.
item.dc:creator: William J. Broad and Cade Metz

item.title: The Liftoff Scenario That Terrifies A.I. Doomsayers
item.description: “Recursive self-improvement” is the idea that artificial intelligence could learn to build and train itself, creating exponential new progress — and risk.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Alana Paterson for The New York Times
item.media:description: Jeff Clune a computer scientist and researcher at the University of British Columbia in Canada and founder of Recursive Superintelligence, one of two $4-billion start-ups chasing recursive self-intelligence.

item.title: Mothers’ Intrusive Thoughts Are Mostly Benign. Lindsay Clancy’s Case Is an Exception.
item.description: Experts say that after childbirth, intrusive thoughts are common and mostly benign. Lindsay Clancy’s story provides a disturbing exception.
item.dc:creator: Ellen Barry

item.title: Does the Stork’s Return to Britain Restore History or Rewrite It?
item.description: Conservationists set up a colony of white storks in southern England, touching off a debate over whether they truly belong there.
item.dc:creator: Leo Sands and Hannah Reyes Morales
item.media:credit: Hannah Reyes Morales for The New York Times

item.title: Is There Anything Google’s Fruit Fly Brain Can’t Do?
item.description: Models of the insect’s nervous system have been trained to solve a Rubik’s Cube, play video games and even parallel park a car.

item.category: Janelia Farm Research Campus (Howard Hughes Medical Institute)

item.title: A T. Rex Walked Here: Teacher Finds Rare Footprints in North Dakota
item.description: Kent Hups, a high school science teacher in Colorado, discovered a 23-foot trackway of fossilized dinosaur footprints, which offer a glimpse of how the apex predator moved 66 million years ago.
item.dc:creator: Adeel Hassan
item.category: Denver Museum of Nature and Science

item.title: Disaster Survivors Sticking Together

item.media:description: Debris from a home destroyed in the Eaton fire in Altadena, Calif., in 2025.

item.title: Harold Freeman, Who Helped Remove Barriers to Cancer Treatment, Dies at 93
item.description: He developed a program that became a model for hospitals around the world, making it easier for poor Black patients to navigate an onerous bureaucratic system.
item.dc:creator: Richard Sandomir
item.category: Lauren, Ralph, Center for Cancer Care and Prevention
item.media:credit: Frances Roberts for The New York Times
item.media:description: Harold Freeman in 2000. Early in his career as a surgeon, he said, he thought he could “cut cancer out of Harlem,” but he soon learned that “the disease would not yield to a surgeon’s knife.”

item.title: FEMA Could Still Lose More Jobs Despite Court Ruling
item.description: A plan to halve the agency’s sprawling work force was illegal, a judge ruled. But the court is not blocking other FEMA cuts.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance
item.media:credit: Al Drago for The New York Times
item.media:description: The headquarters of the Federal Emergency Management Agency in Washington, D.C.

item.title: U.S. Has Deployed Weapons in Space, Air Force Secretary Says

item.media:description: Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink speaks during the United States Air Force Academy graduation ceremony in Colorado Springs in May.

item.title: Could Your Chatbot Be Stealing Ideas From You? It’s a Thorny Question.
item.description: A controversy around OpenAI’s latest math proof raises a fear that might become increasingly common: that A.I. tools could take valuable insights from one user and hand them to another.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Kaoly Gutierrez for The New York Times
item.media:description: If someone types information into a chatbot, those details could turn up — days, months or years later — in a future iteration of that model.

item.title: August Ties for Hottest Month on Record

item.title: States File 2 Lawsuits Over Trump’s Cuts to Endangered Species Act

item.title: Scientists Discover the Earliest Evidence of Drug Use in Really Old Teeth
